```{r}
#| include: false
source("binary_extension_shared.R", local = knitr::knit_global())
```

These notes accompany the [binary outcomes design](design_binary_extension.html).
They document the comparison with the Cro et al. reference implementation,
the rationale for joint latent imputation, and the alternatives considered
for Firth regression.

## Cro et al. latent multivariate probit reference implementation {#sec-binary-probit-validation}

The file `cro_latent_mvn_reference.R` preserves the supplementary code and
trial-specific analysis from @Cro2025. The runnable wrapper in `cro_latent_mvn.R`
exposes the sampler settings as arguments and returns binary imputations
(`imp`), latent draws (`impZ`), and retained arm-specific regression and
covariance draws (`beta` and `omega`). It converts `Ycat` to a data frame so
factor levels are retained when the caller passes a matrix. The wrapper
requires `jomo`, `mice`, and `gear`. The short example can use the CRAN release
of `jomo`.

### Prepare the longitudinal binary outcomes

Both documents use the same trial inputs. `Ycat` has one row per patient,
one column per scheduled visit, and `NA` for missing responses. The threshold
is a reduction of more than 50% from baseline HAMD17. `treat1` codes Placebo
as 1 and Active as 2.

```{r}
#| label: load-cro-reference
source("cro_latent_mvn.R")
```

### Run a short example

This short jump-to-reference (J2R) run illustrates the output of the
intercept-only sampler with monotone dropout and reference arm 1. For the
supplementary settings, use `nburn = 500`, `nbetween = 500`, and `nimp = 1000`.
The `seed` argument defaults to the original seed of 123435. The supplementary
code uses $Y=0$ when $Z>0$. The posterior comparison below reverses the reference
coefficients to match the design's sign convention.

```{r}
#| label: run-cro-probit-example
cro_draws <- cro_latent_mvn(
    Ycat = Ycat,
    treat1 = treat1,
    Method = "J2R",
    Reference = 1,
    nburn = 100,
    nbetween = 10,
    nimp = 5,
    seed = 123435
)
# Imputation 0 contains the original data; positive indices are completed data.
cro_completed <- subset(cro_draws$imp, Imputation == 1)
stopifnot(
    nrow(cro_completed) == nrow(Ycat),
    !anyNA(cro_completed[colnames(Ycat)]),
    all(as.matrix(cro_completed[colnames(Ycat)])[!is.na(Ycat)] ==
        Ycat[!is.na(Ycat)])
)
knitr::kable(
    aggregate(week8 ~ Imputation + Treat,
        data = cro_draws$imp,
        FUN = mean, subset = Imputation > 0
    ),
    caption = "Week 8 response proportions in the short J2R example"
)
# Dimensions of the retained parameter draws.
dim(cro_draws$beta$reference)
dim(cro_draws$omega$active)
```

For incomplete patients, `impZ` contains sequential latent draws at all visits;
its imputation-0 block contains the original binary data, and complete patients'
latent rows remain zero in the supplied algorithm. Use latent rows only for
patients with missing outcomes and positive imputation indices.

### Reference draw sampler

The corrected reference sampler is maintained in the
[rpact-com/jomo fork](https://github.com/rpact-com/jomo). Install the fork in
the default R library and the original CRAN version in a separate library for
comparison:

```r
remotes::install_github("rpact-com/jomo")
dir.create("/tmp/rbmi-jomo-original-library", recursive = TRUE, showWarnings = FALSE)
remotes::install_version("jomo", version = "2.7-6", lib = "/tmp/rbmi-jomo-original-library")
```

Then run from the rbmi repository root:

```bash
RBMI_JOMO_ORIGINAL_LIBRARY=/tmp/rbmi-jomo-original-library RBMI_RUN_PROBIT_VALIDATION=true quarto render misc/research_binary_extension.qmd --to html
```

The validation requires `cmdstanr` with a working CmdStan C++ toolchain,
`posterior`, `mvtnorm`, and `callr`. The installation commands use `remotes`
and require an R package compilation toolchain. The comparison uses CRAN
`jomo` 2.7-6 and the corrected fork (2.7.6.9000). The ordinary render runs
the short example and retains the recorded validation results. The command
above also reruns the Stan fit, reference chains, and independent checks.

```{r}
#| label: probit-run-settings
run_probit_validation <- identical(Sys.getenv("RBMI_RUN_PROBIT_VALIDATION"), "true")
original_library <- Sys.getenv("RBMI_JOMO_ORIGINAL_LIBRARY")
if (run_probit_validation && !dir.exists(file.path(original_library, "jomo"))) {
    stop("Set RBMI_JOMO_ORIGINAL_LIBRARY to the library containing original jomo.")
}
```

#### Fit the Stan model on the same inputs

Fit the Stan model to the trial data and extract paired draws of the coefficients
and correlation matrices.

```{r}
#| label: fit-probit-trial
#| eval: !expr run_probit_validation
probit_model <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(cmdstanr::write_stan_file(probit_stan_code))
probit_input <- prepare_probit_data(Ycat, treat1, same_cov = FALSE)
stopifnot(probit_input$data$R == 831L, probit_input$data$U == 631L)
probit_fit <- fit_probit_draws(probit_input, probit_model, init = 0)
probit_fit$fit$diagnostic_summary()
probit_fit$fit$summary(c("beta", "Omega"))
probit_parameters <- extract_probit_draws(probit_fit, n_samples = 1000L)
stopifnot(
    length(probit_parameters$beta) == 1000L,
    length(probit_parameters$sigma[[1]]) == 2L
)
```

The recorded antidepressant trial fit took about seven minutes.

#### Run the reference chains

The comparison calls `jomo::jomo1cat.MCMCchain()` separately by arm,
matching the draw stage of `cro_latent_mvn()`. Both samplers use the same
200 patients, observed visits, and strict greater-than-50% response threshold.
The comparison uses the retained model parameters before reference-based
imputation.

The [rpact-com/jomo fork](https://github.com/rpact-com/jomo) contains the
corrections used for the binary reference comparison. Their rationale, scope,
and regression tests are documented in the fork's
[changelog](https://github.com/rpact-com/jomo/blob/master/CHANGELOG.md).
The intended binary model uses a flat mean prior and a flat prior on the free
correlations, consistent with Section 3.3 and LKJ(1). The fork preserves those
priors. This document uses the fork as a package dependency; each reference
run loads its selected package in a separate R process.

```{r}
#| label: reference-draw-functions
run_reference_chain <- function(chain, input) {
    set.seed(input$seed + chain)
    lapply(seq_len(nlevels(factor(input$arm))), function(a) {
        yy <- as.data.frame(input$Y[as.integer(factor(input$arm)) == a, , drop = FALSE])
        yy[] <- lapply(yy, factor, levels = 0:1)
        # Mirrors Cro's two draw-stage jomo calls; no reference-based imputation.
        f <- jomo::jomo1cat.MCMCchain(
            Y.cat = yy, Y.numcat = rep(2L, ncol(yy)),
            nburn = input$warmup + input$iterations, output = 0
        )
        take <- seq.int(input$warmup + input$thin,
            input$warmup + input$iterations,
            by = input$thin
        )
        list(
            beta = f$collectbeta[, , take, drop = FALSE],
            omega = f$collectomega[, , take, drop = FALSE]
        )
    })
}

run_reference_draws <- function(Y, arm, library = NULL, chains = 4L,
                                warmup = 100000L, iterations = 1000000L,
                                thin = 100L, seed = 123435L) {
    stopifnot(
        ncol(Y) >= 2L, length(arm) == nrow(Y), !anyNA(arm),
        all(Y[!is.na(Y)] %in% 0:1), chains >= 1L,
        warmup >= 1L, iterations >= thin, thin >= 1L
    )
    # This comparison adapter deliberately stays within Cro's example scope.
    for (a in unique(arm)) {
        yy <- Y[arm == a, , drop = FALSE]
        stopifnot(
            anyNA(yy), all(rowSums(!is.na(yy)) > 0L),
            all(vapply(seq_len(ncol(yy)), function(j) {
                all(0:1 %in% yy[, j])
            }, logical(1)))
        )
    }
    expected_version <- if (is.null(library)) "2.7.6.9000" else "2.7.6"
    input <- list(
        Y = Y, arm = arm, library = library, version = expected_version,
        chains = chains,
        warmup = warmup, iterations = iterations, thin = thin, seed = seed
    )
    callr::r(function(input, run_chain) {
        if (!is.null(input$library)) .libPaths(c(input$library, .libPaths()))
        stopifnot(as.character(utils::packageVersion("jomo")) == input$version)
        cores <- if (.Platform$OS.type == "windows") 1L else input$chains
        out <- parallel::mclapply(seq_len(input$chains), run_chain,
            input = input, mc.cores = cores
        )
        if (any(vapply(out, inherits, logical(1), "try-error"))) {
            stop("Reference chain failed")
        }
        out
    }, args = list(input = input, run_chain = run_reference_chain))
}
```

The reference runner discards 100,000 sweeps and retains every 100th sweep from
one million subsequent sweeps, for each of four independent chains per arm.
This thinning limits storage; it does not establish independence. Correlation
mixing, rather than coefficient mixing, determines how long these runs need to
be. All signs, parameter ordering, MCSEs, and diagnostics are harmonized below.
The comparison includes all ten coefficients and twenty distinct correlations;
constant diagonal entries and duplicated upper triangles are excluded.

```{r}
#| label: compare-probit-functions
jomo_array <- function(chains) {
    S <- dim(chains[[1]][[1]]$beta)[3]
    A <- length(chains[[1]])
    D <- dim(chains[[1]][[1]]$omega)[1]
    pair <- which(lower.tri(matrix(0, D, D)), arr.ind = TRUE)
    nm <- c(paste0("beta[", seq_len(A * D), "]"), unlist(lapply(seq_len(A), function(a) {
        sprintf("Omega[%d,%d,%d]", a, pair[, 1], pair[, 2])
    })))
    arr <- array(NA_real_, c(S, length(chains), length(nm)), dimnames = list(NULL, NULL, nm))
    for (ch in seq_along(chains)) {
        values <- c(
            lapply(seq_len(A), function(a) -t(chains[[ch]][[a]]$beta[1, , ])),
            lapply(seq_len(A), function(a) {
                t(vapply(seq_len(S), function(s) {
                    chains[[ch]][[a]]$omega[, , s][pair]
                }, numeric(nrow(pair))))
            })
        )
        arr[, ch, ] <- do.call(cbind, values)
    }
    posterior::as_draws_array(arr)
}
summarize_parameters <- function(draws) {
    as.data.frame(posterior::summarise_draws(draws,
        mean = mean, sd = sd,
        q025 = function(x) unname(quantile(x, .025)),
        q975 = function(x) unname(quantile(x, .975)),
        mcse = posterior::mcse_mean, rhat = posterior::rhat,
        ess_bulk = posterior::ess_bulk, ess_tail = posterior::ess_tail
    ))
}
compare_parameters <- function(stan, reference) {
    a <- summarize_parameters(stan)
    b <- summarize_parameters(reference)
    z <- merge(a, b, by = "variable", suffixes = c("_stan", "_reference"), sort = FALSE)
    z$difference <- z$mean_stan - z$mean_reference
    z$combined_mcse <- sqrt(z$mcse_stan^2 + z$mcse_reference^2)
    z$mcse_units <- z$difference / z$combined_mcse
    z$sd_units <- z$difference / z$sd_stan
    z
}
```

```{r}
#| label: compare-probit-reference
#| eval: !expr run_probit_validation
reference_original <- run_reference_draws(Ycat, treat1, library = original_library)
reference_corrected <- run_reference_draws(Ycat, treat1)
comparison_original <- compare_parameters(
    probit_fit$fit$draws(c("beta", "Omega")), jomo_array(reference_original)
)
comparison_corrected <- compare_parameters(
    probit_fit$fit$draws(c("beta", "Omega")), jomo_array(reference_corrected)
)
knitr::kable(
    comparison_corrected[, c(
        "variable", "mean_stan", "mean_reference",
        "difference", "combined_mcse", "mcse_units"
    )],
    digits = 4
)
# Also inspect posterior SDs, interval endpoints, R-hat, and both ESS estimates:
comparison_corrected
```

### Recorded comparison (26 October 2026)

This snapshot used R 4.6.1, CmdStanR 0.9.0, CmdStan 2.39.0, posterior 1.7.0,
and jomo 2.7-6 with the two corrections now maintained in the
[rpact-com/jomo fork](https://github.com/rpact-com/jomo). These recorded results
predate the fork's development version; they have not been recomputed for this
source migration. Stan used four chains, 1,500 warmup iterations per chain,
and 2,000 retained sampling iterations per chain after the step-size cap;
its warmup seed was 20261026 and sampling seed 20261027. Both reference
runs used four chains per arm with seeds 123436 through 123439, 100,000
burn-in sweeps, and one million further sweeps, retaining every 100th.

**The corrected reference agrees with the paper-targeted Stan model:** the largest
absolute posterior-mean difference was 2.09 combined MCSEs across all 30 parameters.
The maximum absolute differences were 0.0036 for coefficients and 0.0062 for correlations.
Posterior SDs differed by at most 2.4%, and the largest difference between
corresponding 95% interval endpoints was 0.150 Stan posterior SDs.
These are Monte Carlo comparisons, not a proof of equality of the two algorithms.

The unmodified reference differs systematically: the placebo Week 1 coefficient
is -1.742 versus -1.956 in Stan (83.0 combined MCSEs). The corrected value is -1.952.
The two corrections described in the fork's changelog were applied together;
this experiment does not attribute every discrepancy separately to either one.

|Sampler        | Maximum R-hat| Minimum bulk ESS| Minimum tail ESS|
|:--------------|-------------:|----------------:|----------------:|
|Stan           |        1.0017|             3441|             4816|
|Corrected jomo |        1.0072|             1320|             1987|
|Original jomo  |        1.0016|             2252|             3399|

Stan had **0 divergent transitions**, 0 maximum-treedepth hits, and E-BFMI
between 0.925 and 0.971 in the retained chains. R-hat and ESS above summarize
only the ten coefficients and twenty distinct correlations. Initial warmup
rejections are not counted as retained-chain divergences. These diagnostics
support this example; they do not guarantee adequate sampling on a new dataset.

All reference coefficients in the following tables have been sign-reversed.
“Difference / MCSE” is $(\bar\theta_{\mathrm{Stan}}-\bar\theta_{\mathrm{corrected}})/
\sqrt{\mathrm{MCSE}_{\mathrm{Stan}}^2+\mathrm{MCSE}_{\mathrm{corrected}}^2}$.
The interval columns describe the Stan posterior, not a Monte Carlo confidence interval.

The independent bivariate identity check had maximum absolute error 3e-15.
For the one-visit example (7 responses among 20 patients), the numerical posterior
mean was -0.392807 versus -0.382052 in Stan (MCSE 0.006725); posterior SDs were 0.289319 and 0.285921.
The log-quantile comparison with R had maximum absolute error 7.1e-15 over log
probabilities from $-10^{-16}$ to $-10^6$. Both the one-visit fit and the
covariate/intermittent-missingness fit had zero divergences and zero treedepth
hits; all seven simulated coefficients were inside their 95% posterior intervals.

## Probit draw model performance

The current implementation parallelizes chains. Further optimizations could be
benchmarked without changing the statistical target:

- **Within-chain parallelism.** The block log-likelihood contributions can be
  summed with Stan's [`reduce_sum`](https://mc-stan.org/docs/stan-users-guide/parallelization.html).
  Replace the running `u_pos` counter with fixed block offsets so each task reads
  the correct auxiliary parameters independently. Visits within a subject must
  remain sequential because their conditional calculations depend on earlier
  values. Compile with `cpp_options = list(stan_threads = TRUE)` and pass
  `threads_per_chain` explicitly to both sampling calls in `fit_probit_draws()`;
  its current `...` reaches only the adaptation stage. Budget cores across
  `parallel_chains * threads_per_chain`.
- **Balance the work.** This example has 11 blocks, but the two largest contain
  61 and 69 complete patients, accounting for 650 of 831 observations. Splitting
  large blocks into smaller subject batches may therefore scale better than
  assigning whole blocks to tasks. Preserve one covariance factorization per
  block and share it across batches, or benchmark the simpler alternative of
  repeating the small factorization within each batch.
- **Reduce serial work and improve sampling efficiency.** For the default
  saturated design, direct coefficient indexing could replace the dense
  `X * beta` multiplication. Alternative visit orders and less conservative
  step-size caps may improve effective samples per second, but require renewed
  divergence, treedepth, E-BFMI, and convergence checks before adoption.
- **Measure before adopting.** Profile the likelihood and benchmark elapsed time
  and effective samples per second with 1, 2, and 4 threads per chain. Start with
  `grainsize = 1`, then tune batch size and grainsize if useful. At this example's
  size, scheduling and automatic-differentiation overhead may outweigh threading
  gains; larger datasets offer more opportunity.

## Independent probit validation checks

The opt-in validation also checks the bivariate orthant identity, the one-visit posterior against
numerical integration, and the data mapping for a covariate-adjusted model with
intermittent missingness and an entirely missing subject. The simulation uses a
shared correlation matrix and checks coverage of the known coefficient vector;
it is a small implementation check, not a simulation study of operating
characteristics. Rejection of flat priors for separated cells or custom designs,
and preservation of matrix dimensions during extraction, are also checked.

```{r}
#| label: validate-probit-independent
#| eval: !expr run_probit_validation
model <- probit_model

# Deterministic two-visit orthant check, including all four sign patterns.
mu <- c(-.7, .3)
Omega <- matrix(c(1, .6, .6, 1), 2)
L <- t(chol(Omega))
signs <- as.matrix(expand.grid(c(-1, 1), c(-1, 1)))
err <- apply(signs, 1, function(s) {
    p1 <- pnorm(s[1] * mu[1])
    value <- integrate(function(u) {
        e1 <- -s[1] * qnorm(u * p1)
        p1 * pnorm(s[2] * (mu[2] + L[2, 1] * e1) / L[2, 2])
    }, 0, 1, rel.tol = 1e-10)$value
    truth <- as.numeric(mvtnorm::pmvnorm(
        lower = c(0, 0),
        upper = c(Inf, Inf), mean = s * mu, sigma = Omega * outer(s, s), algorithm = mvtnorm::TVPACK()
    ))
    value - truth
})
stopifnot(max(abs(err)) < 1e-8)

# One visit: no augmentation variables; compare against numerical quadrature.
y <- matrix(c(rep(1, 7), rep(0, 13)), ncol = 1)
p <- prepare_probit_data(y, rep(1, nrow(y)))
stopifnot(p$data$U == 0L, p$data$R == 20L, p$data$P == 1L)
f <- fit_probit_draws(p, model, chains = 4, iter_warmup = 500, iter_sampling = 2000, seed = 883L)
sm <- summarize_parameters(f$fit$draws("beta"))
density <- function(b) exp(7 * pnorm(b, log.p = TRUE) + 13 * pnorm(-b, log.p = TRUE))
constant <- integrate(density, -Inf, Inf)$value
exact_mean <- integrate(function(b) b * density(b), -Inf, Inf)$value / constant
exact_sd <- sqrt(integrate(function(b) (b - exact_mean)^2 * density(b), -Inf, Inf)$value / constant)
stopifnot(
    abs(sm$mean - exact_mean) < 4 * sm$mcse,
    abs(sm$sd - exact_sd) < .02
)
ex <- extract_probit_draws(f, 10)
stopifnot(
    length(ex$beta) == 10L, length(ex$sigma) == 10L,
    identical(dim(ex$sigma[[1]][[1]]), c(1L, 1L)),
    ex$sigma[[1]][[1]][1, 1] == 1
)

# Data preparation: arbitrary missing patterns, all-missing subjects, custom X.
set.seed(443)
N <- 180L
D <- 3L
arm <- rep(1:2, each = N / 2)
x <- rnorm(N)
X <- array(0, c(N, D, 7L))
for (i in seq_len(N)) {
    for (j in seq_len(D)) {
        X[i, j, j] <- 1
        X[i, j, 3 + j] <- arm[i] == 2
        X[i, j, 7] <- x[i]
    }
}
truth <- c(-.6, -.3, .1, .4, .5, .6, .3)
Sigma <- matrix(c(1, .55, .3, .55, 1, .4, .3, .4, 1), 3)
eta <- matrix(matrix(X, N * D, 7L) %*% truth, N, D)
Z <- eta + matrix(rnorm(N * D), N, D) %*% chol(Sigma)
Y <- 1L * (Z > 0)
Y[matrix(runif(N * D) < .2, N, D)] <- NA
Y[1, ] <- NA
p2 <- prepare_probit_data(Y, arm, X, same_cov = TRUE, beta_sd = 2)
stopifnot(
    1L %in% p2$excluded_subjects, p2$data$G == 1L,
    all(p2$data$sign_y == 2 * Y[p2$cells] - 1),
    isTRUE(all.equal(p2$data$X,
        sapply(1:7, function(k) matrix(X[, , k], N, D)[p2$cells]),
        check.attributes = FALSE
    ))
)
stopifnot(
    inherits(try(prepare_probit_data(Y, arm, X, beta_sd = 0), silent = TRUE), "try-error"),
    inherits(try(prepare_probit_data(matrix(0, 10, 2), rep(1, 10)), silent = TRUE), "try-error")
)
f2 <- fit_probit_draws(p2, model, chains = 4, iter_warmup = 1000, iter_sampling = 1500, seed = 884L)
sm2 <- summarize_parameters(f2$fit$draws("beta"))
stopifnot(
    all(sm2$rhat < 1.01), all(sm2$ess_bulk > 400),
    all(truth > sm2$q025 & truth < sm2$q975)
)

list(
    bivariate_errors = err, univariate = cbind(sm, exact_mean, exact_sd),
    synthetic = cbind(sm2, truth)
)
f$fit$diagnostic_summary()
f2$fit$diagnostic_summary()
```

The log-quantile helper is checked separately against R's tail-aware `qnorm`,
including probabilities whose ordinary floating-point representation underflows.
Writing Stan's output at 18 significant figures is necessary for this numerical
check; rounding CSV output must not be mistaken for function error.

```{r}
#| label: validate-probit-log-quantile
#| eval: !expr run_probit_validation
code <- strsplit(probit_stan_code, "\n", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
code <- code[seq_len(which(code == "data {")[1] - 1L)]
code <- c(
    code, "data { int<lower=1> N; vector[N] lp; }",
    "generated quantities { vector[N] q; for (i in 1:N) q[i] = std_normal_quantile_log(lp[i]); }"
)
m <- cmdstanr::cmdstan_model(cmdstanr::write_stan_file(code))
lp <- c(-1e-16, -1e-10, -.1, log(.5), -2, -36 + 1e-8, -36 - 1e-8, -50, -100, -700, -1000, -1e6)
f <- m$sample(data = list(N = length(lp), lp = lp), fixed_param = TRUE, chains = 1, iter_sampling = 1, refresh = 0, sig_figs = 18)
q <- as.numeric(posterior::as_draws_matrix(f$draws("q"))[1, ])
truth <- qnorm(lp, log.p = TRUE)
z <- data.frame(lp, q, truth, error = q - truth)
print(z)
stopifnot(max(abs(z$error)) < 1e-9)
```

## Reference-based imputation

### Original imputation algorithm {#sec-binary-original-imputation}

Section 3.3 of @Cro2025 samples latent responses in visit order. The steps
below use the design's sign convention, $Y_j=\mathbf{1}(Z_j>0)$, and
suppress the patient and arm indices.

1. Use a single joint posterior draw to construct the patient's mean vector
   $\mu$ and covariance matrix $\Sigma$ under the selected
   [reference assumption](design_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-reference-distribution).
2. At the first visit, where the original algorithm assumes an observed
   response, draw $Z_1$ from its truncated marginal normal distribution.
   The sign is positive for a response and negative for a nonresponse.
3. At each subsequent visit $j$, let $S=\{1,\ldots,j-1\}$ index the
   previously sampled latent responses. The conditional normal mean and
   variance are

   $$
   \begin{aligned}
   m_{j\mid S} &= \mu_j+\Sigma_{jS}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}(Z_S-\mu_S),\\
   v_{j\mid S} &= \Sigma_{jj}-\Sigma_{jS}\Sigma_{SS}^{-1}\Sigma_{Sj}.
   \end{aligned}
   $$

   At the second visit, these reduce to
   $m_{2\mid1}=\mu_2+\Sigma_{21}(Z_1-\mu_1)/\Sigma_{11}$ and
   $v_{2\mid1}=\Sigma_{22}-\Sigma_{21}^2/\Sigma_{11}$. Draw $Z_j$ from
   this conditional normal if the response is missing. If the response is
   observed, sample $Z_j$ with truncation to the observed sign. Earlier
   draws stay fixed.

The [corrected algorithm](design_binary_extension.html#sec-binary-joint-sampling)
conditions on all observed signs jointly.

### Problem in the original algorithm

The original sampler accepts each observed sign by resampling only the current
latent variable, leaving earlier draws unchanged. Direct univariate truncated
normal sampling is equivalent to that local rejection step, but neither
conditions earlier latent values on later observed signs. To see why, consider
two observed responses $Y_1=Y_2=1$. Hold the model parameters fixed and suppress
the patient index and reference-assumption superscript. Let
$\phi(z_1;\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})$ denote the marginal normal density of $Z_1$.

1. Under our sign convention, observing $Y_1=Y_2=1$ is the event
   $E=\{Z_1>0,Z_2>0\}$. Bayes' rule for the density of $Z_1$ conditional on
   this event gives
   $$
   p(z_1\mid E)
   =\frac{p(z_1)\Pr(E\mid Z_1=z_1)}{\Pr(E)}.
   $$
   Here conditioning on $Z_1=z_1$ uses the conditional distribution of $Z_2$;
   it does not require the point event $\{Z_1=z_1\}$ to have positive probability.

2. Once $Z_1=z_1$ is fixed, the first sign is already determined. If $z_1\leq0$,
   the event $E$ is impossible; if $z_1>0$, only the second sign remains uncertain.
   Therefore
   $$
   \Pr(E\mid Z_1=z_1)
   =\mathbf{1}(z_1>0)\Pr(Z_2>0\mid Z_1=z_1).
   $$

3. Substitute this expression and the marginal normal density into Bayes' rule:
   $$
   p(z_1\mid Y_1=1,Y_2=1)
   =\frac{
     \phi(z_1;\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})\mathbf{1}(z_1>0)
     \Pr(Z_2>0\mid Z_1=z_1)
   }{\Pr(Z_1>0,Z_2>0)}.
   $$
   The denominator is constant with respect to $z_1$, so dropping it gives

$$
p(z_1\mid Y_1=1,Y_2=1)\propto
\phi(z_1;\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})\mathbf{1}(z_1>0)
\Pr(Z_2>0\mid Z_1=z_1).
$$

The extra factor can be written explicitly using normal conditioning. Define

$$
\mu_{2\mid1}(z_1)=\mu_2+
\frac{\Sigma_{21}}{\Sigma_{11}}(z_1-\mu_1),\qquad
s_{2\mid1}^2=\Sigma_{22}-\frac{\Sigma_{21}^2}{\Sigma_{11}}.
$$

Then $Z_2\mid Z_1=z_1\sim N(\mu_{2\mid1}(z_1),s_{2\mid1}^2)$, and hence

$$
\Pr(Z_2>0\mid Z_1=z_1)
=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{-\mu_{2\mid1}(z_1)}{s_{2\mid1}}\right)
=\Phi\!\left(\frac{\mu_{2\mid1}(z_1)}{s_{2\mid1}}\right).
$$

By contrast, drawing $Z_1$ from its marginal normal truncated above zero uses
only $p(z_1\mid Y_1=1)\propto
\phi(z_1;\mu_1,\Sigma_{11})\mathbf{1}(z_1>0)$. It omits the probability of
the second observed sign. With positive correlation, larger $z_1$ makes
$Z_2>0$ more likely, so observing $Y_2=1$ gives those larger values additional
weight. If the correlation is zero, this factor is constant and cancels in
normalization; in general it depends on $z_1$ and cannot be omitted.

Consequently,
a single forward pass is not a joint truncated-normal draw, even with monotone
dropout. This is a limitation of the paper's Step 5 as written, not a consequence
of replacing its local rejection sampler with inverse-CDF sampling. The simple
case of one observed visit followed only by missing visits does not have this
problem.

As a numerical example, take three zero-mean latent variables with unit
variances and all correlations $\rho=0.7$, and observe $Y=(1,1,\mathrm{NA})$.
The exact conditional response probability, using the bivariate and trivariate
zero-mean normal orthant identities, is

$$
\Pr(Y_3=1\mid Y_1=Y_2=1)
=\frac{1/8+3\arcsin(\rho)/(4\pi)}{1/4+\arcsin(\rho)/(2\pi)}
=0.8304917.
$$

The following base-R example compares the original sampler with whole-vector
rejection, which is an exact joint sampler and is inexpensive for this particular
orthant. For the sequential estimate we integrate out the last normal draw to
reduce Monte Carlo noise. The sequential estimate is about 0.811, versus 0.8305
for the target; the discrepancy is much larger than Monte Carlo error.

```{r}
#| label: compare-sequential-joint-imputation
local({
    set.seed(917)
    n <- 1000000L
    rho <- 0.7
    Sigma <- matrix(rho, 3, 3)
    diag(Sigma) <- 1
    exact <- (1 / 8 + 3 * asin(rho) / (4 * pi)) /
        (1 / 4 + asin(rho) / (2 * pi))

    # Joint rejection: reject the entire vector unless both observed signs match.
    z <- matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n, 3) %*% chol(Sigma)
    joint_response <- z[z[, 1] > 0 & z[, 2] > 0, 3] > 0

    # Original forward sampler: independently enforce each successive sign.
    z1 <- -qnorm(runif(n) / 2)
    m2 <- rho * z1
    s2 <- sqrt(1 - rho^2)
    z2 <- m2 - s2 * qnorm(runif(n) * pnorm(m2 / s2))
    b <- drop(Sigma[3, 1:2] %*% solve(Sigma[1:2, 1:2]))
    v3 <- Sigma[3, 3] - sum(b * Sigma[1:2, 3])
    sequential_probability <- pnorm((b[1] * z1 + b[2] * z2) / sqrt(v3))

    data.frame(
        Method = c("Exact", "Joint rejection", "Original sequential"),
        Probability = c(exact, mean(joint_response), mean(sequential_probability)),
        MCSE = c(
            0, sd(joint_response) / sqrt(length(joint_response)),
            sd(sequential_probability) / sqrt(n)
        )
    )
})
```

### Choice of joint sampler {#sec-binary-sampler-choice}

`tmvtnorm` [@Wilhelm2010] supports whole-vector rejection and Gibbs sampling.
Ordinary rejection becomes expensive for rare observed sign patterns; Gibbs
requires burn-in and mixing checks, particularly under strong correlations.
Its updates condition on all other current latent coordinates and must be
iterated to convergence; one forward pass is not a substitute.
See the [current package documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/CRAN/web/packages/tmvtnorm/refman/tmvtnorm.html#rtmvnorm).

`TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm()` implements Botev's minimax exponential tilting
accept-reject method [@Botev2017]. It targets
independent draws without Gibbs burn-in and accepts infinite bounds, so observed
and missing coordinates can be handled together. This is a provisional choice
for the intended range of **5 to 30 visits**, not a claim of uniformly best
performance. See the [package overview](https://lbelzile.github.io/TruncatedNormal/)
and [sampling API](https://lbelzile.github.io/TruncatedNormal/reference/rtmvnorm.html).
For this illustration, the patient has a response at the first visit,
no observation at the second, and a nonresponse at the third.

```{r}
#| label: joint-imputation-sampler-call
set.seed(928L)
y <- c(1L, NA_integer_, 0L)
mu_ref <- c(0, 0.2, 0)
Sigma_ref <- matrix(0.5, 3, 3)
diag(Sigma_ref) <- 1

lower <- rep(-Inf, length(y))
upper <- rep(Inf, length(y))
lower[which(y == 1)] <- 0
upper[which(y == 0)] <- 0
z <- as.numeric(TruncatedNormal::rtmvnorm(
    n = 1, mu = mu_ref, sigma = Sigma_ref, lb = lower, ub = upper
))
completed <- y
completed[is.na(y)] <- as.integer(z[is.na(y)] > 0)
completed
```

Before selecting a production backend, benchmark 5, 10, 20, and 30 visits across
posterior draws with common and rare sign patterns, weak and strong correlations,
and varying fractions of missing visits. Measure setup plus sampling time per
patient per imputation, numerical failures, and accuracy against orthant
probabilities or small-dimensional rejection checks; for MCMC also measure
burn-in and effective sample size. Compare full-vector tilting with the
observed-block/conditional-Gaussian factorization. Matrix factorizations can be
reused where covariance and coordinate patterns agree, but tilting optimization
also depends on the centered bounds, which vary with means and observed signs.
The [implementation](https://github.com/lbelzile/TruncatedNormal/blob/master/R/mvrandn.R)
can warn about solver failure, near-singularity, or low acceptance and can return
fewer draws than requested; production code must detect these cases rather than
silently accepting the output. Hamiltonian alternatives such as
[`hdtg`](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.01097) are worth considering if these benchmarks
show a bottleneck, but their published advantages concern much higher dimensions
and do not establish superiority at 20--30 visits.

## Firth regression alternatives {#sec-binary-firth-research}

| Implementation | Fit and extraction | Trade-off for `rbmi` |
|---|---|---|
| From scratch | Use the closed form for the unadjusted two-arm model or the adjusted-score algorithm below when the model includes covariates. | Dependency-free. An adjusted solver needs numerical safeguards and validation against reference fits. |
| `logistf` | Use `logistf::logistf(formula, data = data, pl = FALSE)` and extract the coefficient and its covariance. | Dedicated Firth implementation with profile penalized-likelihood intervals available. The Wald option fits the existing coefficient-and-SE pooling interface. See the [logistf manual](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/logistf/html/logistf.html). |
| `brglm2` | Use `glm(formula, data = data, family = binomial(), method = brglm2::brglmFit, type = "AS_mean")` and extract with `coef()` and `vcov()`. | Mean bias reduction gives the Firth estimate for logistic regression and keeps the familiar GLM interface for covariate-adjusted analyses. See the [brglm2 fitting documentation](https://search.r-project.org/CRAN/refmans/brglm2/html/brglmFit.html). |

**Scope of the closed form.** The two-by-two shortcut applies to a model
with an intercept and a two-level treatment indicator only. The
arm-by-response counts fully describe this model because everyone in an
arm shares one fitted probability.
With an adjustment variable such as baseline severity, fitted probabilities
can vary within an arm, so the two-by-two table no longer contains the
information needed for the fit.

### Extending the callback to adjust for covariates

To extend the current treatment-only callback, build an endpoint model such
as `outcome ~ group + baseline`, fit it with `logistf` or `brglm2`, and
extract the treatment coefficient and its
standard error for the specified reference arm. Return `est`, `se`, and the
residual degrees of freedom (the number of analyzed subjects minus the model
matrix rank) in the existing format. `binary_analyse()` and `rbmi::pool()` can
then use that result as before. The treatment coefficient is a conditional
log odds ratio at fixed covariate values. The covariates must already be
available for analysis in each completed dataset.

Most of the package integration effort would go into checking missing
covariates, consistent factor coding and an estimable treatment contrast
across imputations, and reporting rank or convergence failures with the
affected imputation index.

### From-scratch algorithm for Firth regression with covariates

For one completed dataset, let $y$ be the $n$ binary outcomes at the endpoint
and $X$ the $n \times p$ model matrix, including the intercept, treatment
indicator and covariate columns. The same algorithm covers the unadjusted
model and models with continuous or categorical covariates.

1. **Initialize.** Check that $X$ is full rank, $n>p$, and all outcomes and
   covariates are available. Start at $\beta=0$, which gives an initial
   probability of $1/2$ without requiring a maximum-likelihood fit.
2. **Compute weights and leverages.** At the current $\beta$, compute
   $\eta=X\beta$, $\mu_i=\operatorname{logit}^{-1}(\eta_i)$, and
   $w_i=\mu_i(1-\mu_i)$. Set $W=\operatorname{diag}(w_i)$ and compute a thin QR
   factorization $W^{1/2}X=QR$. Compute $h_i=\sum_j Q_{ij}^2$, the leverage
   of subject $i$. Use row scaling for $W^{1/2}X$ and row sums of squares for
   the leverages so neither $W$ nor the hat matrix has to be allocated.
3. **Compute the adjusted score and direction.** Form
   $U^*=X^\top\{y-\mu+h(1/2-\mu)\}$, with the multiplication by $h$
   elementwise. Solve $R^\top R\,\Delta=U^*$ using two triangular solves,
   since $R^\top R=I(\beta)=X^\top W X$. This is a quasi-Fisher scoring
   step. If the QR implementation pivots the columns, apply the same
   permutation to the score and undo it for the coefficient update.
4. **Update with backtracking.** Try $\beta+\Delta$. If the trial point
   has a numerically singular weighted design or decreases the penalized
   log-likelihood, halve the step and retry. Evaluate the Bernoulli
   log-likelihood stably from the linear predictors and compute the
   half log-determinant penalty as $\sum_j\log |R_{jj}|$ at each trial point.
   Stop when the information-scaled score $\|R^{-\top}U^*\|_2$ and the
   relative size of the full scoring direction meet their tolerances. Using
   the full direction prevents declaring convergence solely because
   backtracking produced a small accepted step. If the line search or
   iteration limit is exhausted, report the failure and its imputation index.
5. **Return the treatment contrast.** For a contrast vector $c$, compute
   $\mathrm{est}=c^\top\hat\beta$ and
   $\mathrm{se}=\sqrt{c^\top I(\hat\beta)^{-1}c}$ using the final QR factor
   and a triangular solve. For the treatment coefficient, $c$ selects its
   column in $X$. Return those values with $\mathrm{df}=n-p$ for Rubin
   pooling.

The adjusted score and scoring direction follow the mean bias reduction
algorithm in [Kosmidis, Kenne Pagui and Sartori (2020)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s11222-019-09860-6).

For a dense design with $n \ge p$, a weighted QR factorization costs
$O(np^2)$ time and $O(np+p^2)$ working memory. The factorization dominates
each scoring iteration and each trial point checked by the line search.
With $M$ imputations and an average of $K$ factorizations per fit, including
backtracking, the total fitting cost is $O(MKnp^2)$ for similarly sized
datasets. With a few covariates this is roughly linear in the number of
subjects and imputations. Those costs are for the endpoint fits and exclude
the draw and imputation steps.

The scoring loop is short with base R linear algebra. A production fitter
is a moderate implementation effort because it must handle extreme linear
predictors, nearly singular weighted designs, and failed line searches while
returning reliable standard errors. Test the unadjusted fit against the
closed form and compare coefficients and standard errors with a reference
package on adjusted data with and without separation. Also verify explicit
failure for rank-deficient designs. A package-backed callback delegates the
solver and leaves the model-matrix, contrast and pooling integration to
`rbmi`.

### Closed-form reference

For arm $g$ with $y_g$ responses among $n_g$ patients, the fitted Firth
probability is $\hat p_g = (y_g + 1/2)/(n_g + 1)$. The log odds ratio is the
difference of the fitted logits, and its within-imputation variance is
$\sum_g [n_g\hat p_g(1-\hat p_g)]^{-1}$. This gives a reference for checking
the package-based fit in the unadjusted two-arm model.
